The learned trial Court held that defendant no.1 had not disputed the sale deed in favour of the plaintiffs.
His plea that the sale deed was a sham transaction, which was never intended to be acted upon was not established.
Defendant No.1 admitted that he had received 4,500/- at the time of the registration of the sale deed.
This falsifies his plea that the sale deed was a sham transaction, and his conduct of not challenging the sale deed since 23.06.1970 also supported this conclusion.

However,
the plaintiffs did not place any tatima on record to show the land purchased by them; therefore, no relief could be granted to them.

The defendants failed to prove their plea of adverse possession.
.
There was a distinction between a long possession and adverse possession.
Long possession cannot be equated to adverse possession.
The sale deed was not binding upon the rights of the plaintiffs to the extent of 2 bighas, 5 biswas.
The tenancy in favour of defendant no.2 by of defendant no.1 did not affect the rights of the plaintiffs.
Learned Trial Court answered Issue No.1 partly in affirmative Issues No. 2, 7(a) and 7 rt (e) in affirmative.

8. Being aggrieved from the judgment and decree passed by the learned Trial Court, the plaintiffs filed an appeal before the learned District Judge.

The legal representatives of defendants no. 1 and 2 also filed an appeal challenging the findings that defendant no.1 had sold 2 bighas 5 biswas of land to the plaintiffs and conferment of proprietary rights in favour of defendant no.2, is illegal, null and void.
An application for leading additional evidence and another for amendment of the plaint was filed by the plaintiffs.
The application for leading additional evidence was allowed, whereas the application for amendment was dismissed.

9. Learned First Appellate Court held that the tatima attached to the sale deed and mutation were proved on record, which showed that .
Khasra No. 83/2 measuring 2-5 bighas was sold to the plaintiffs.
The sale was of a specific portion of the land.
The plea taken by defendant no.1 regarding the sale deed being a sham transaction and that he remained in possession was not proved.
The portion of Khasra No. 83 of was acquired by the State of H.P. for widening the road.
A perusal of the tatima depicting the portion acquired by the State of H.P. shows that the rt land was divided horizontally, whereas it was divided vertically in the sale deed.
Hence, 1 bigha 1 biswas of land was acquired by the State of H.P. from the share of the plaintiffs and plaintiffs remained in possession of 1-4 bighas after the acquisition.
This was corroborated by the letter written by defendant no.2, Prem Chand.
The findings recorded by the learned Trial Court regarding the defendants not having proved the adverse possession were upheld.

Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Trial Court,
the present appeal has been filed asserting that the learned First Appellate Court erred in holding that 1-1 bighas of land was acquired from the share of the plaintiffs.
The of application for amendment was wrongly rejected against the well-settled principles of law.
The plaintiffs were entitled to a relief of joint rt possession in respect of 2-5 bighas of land, especially when Sher Singh had taken the compensation for the acquisition of the land.

11. The appeal was admitted on the following substantial questions of law:-
"1.

Whether wrong assumptions have been drawn from the facts proved on record and the findings are based on inadmissible oral and documentary evidence particularly the letters stated to have been written by the appellant to Sher Singh,
which have been used without being proved.

2. Whether the District Judge was right in disallowing the amendment of the plaint and the findings are bad and against the well-settled principles for grant of an amendment which was necessary for determining the controversy between the parties?"

It was duly proved that the compensation was taken by defendant no. 1;
rt therefore, defendant no.1 is liable to compensate the plaintiffs by making good the land for which he had taken the compensation.
Learned First Appellate Court erred in not considering this aspect.

The learned First Appellate Court relied upon the letter written by the defendant to the plaintiffs,
but this document was not proved as per the law and could not have been considered.
The learned First Appellate Court erred in rejecting the application for amendment.

Hence, he prayed that the present appeal be allowed, and the judgment and decree passed by learned First Appellate Court be set aside.

suit and declare the plaintiffs to be the owner of 2-5 bighas of land.
Learned First Appellate court had carefully analysed the evidence on record and no interference is required with the same.

15. Sh. Bhupender Gupta learned senior counsel for of respondents no. 1 to 5 original defendant No.2 and Sh. Bimal Gupta, learned Senior Counsel for respondent no.15 original defendant No.3 rt supported the judgment and decree passed by the learned First Appellate Court and submitted that no interferences is acquired with the same.
16. I have given considerable thought to the rival submissions at the bar and have gone through the records carefully.

Substantial questions of law no.1.
17.
Learned first Appellate Court relied upon the letter (Mark B) written by the defendant to plaintiff, Prem Chand to hold that the land purchased by the plaintiffs was acquired by the State.
It held that this letter was put to defendant no. 1 by the plaintiffs in the cross- examination and, the letter could be used against them.
The letter could not be read against the defendant, as the same was not proved as per the law.
A perusal of the testimony of Sher Singh (DW-1) shows that the letter (Mark B) was put to him.
He denied his signatures on this letter or the fact that he had written the document.
Therefore, learned First .
Appellate Court had rightly held that this document was put by the plaintiffs to the defendant.
18. It was submitted that the learned First Appellate Court erred in relying upon a document, which was not proved as per the law of by examining the executant.
This submission cannot be accepted.

It was laid down by the Delhi High Court in Rudnap Export-Import v.
rt Eastern Associates Co., 1983 SCC OnLine Del 136 = AIR 1984 Delhi 20 that no evidence is required to prove the document produced by the party and it can be read against him.

19. No precedent to the contrary was brought to the notice of this Court; therefore, the learned First Appellate Court had rightly relied upon the document, which was produced by the plaintiffs and was put to of defendant no.1 in the cross-examination.
There is no infirmity in placing reliance upon this document.
Hence, this substantial question of law is rt answered accordingly.
Substantial question of law no. 2 20.
The plaintiffs filed an application under Order 6 Rule 17 of CPC for seeking the amendment of the plaint.

It was asserted that the learned Trial Court held that the plaintiffs were owners in possession of 2-5 bighas of land out of Khasra No. 83, but not in possession of Khasra No.83/2 or any other part of Khasra No. 83, the mutation no. 252 conferring the proprietary rights over the land bearing Khasra No. 83/2/1 is illegal, null and void and the sale deed no. 138 was bad.
Total measurement of Khasra No.83 was 5-18 bighas out of which 2-3 bigha was acquired by the State of Himachal Pradesh and 2-5 bigha was purchased by plaintiff Sher Singh.
Hence, it had become necessary to incorporate this fact in the plaint.
A relief of joint possession of the land was also sought.

This application was opposed by the defendants by filing a written statement taking preliminary objection regarding lack of maintainability and the applicants being estopped by their act and conduct to file the present suit.
The contents of the application were of denied on merits.
It was asserted that a specific portion was purchased by the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs cannot claim to be the purchasers of rt the joint land.

Hence, it was prayed that the application be dismissed.

It was held:
"4. The short question, which arises for consideration of is as to whether the proviso appended to Order VI, Rule 17 of the Code is applicable in the instant case.
5. Order VI, Rule 17 of the Code reads, thus:
rt "The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties."
6.
Proviso appended thereto was added by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2002 which came into force with effect from 1.07.2002.

It reads as under:
"Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial has commenced unless the Court comes to the conclusion that in spite of due diligence,
the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement of trial."
7. Section 16(2) of the Amending Act of 2002 reads as under:
"16(2) Notwithstanding that the provisions of this Act have come into force or repeal under sub-section (1) has taken effect, and without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 _ (a) *** *** .
(b) the provisions of rules 5, 15, 17 and 18 of Order VI of the First Schedule as omitted or, as the case may be, inserted or substituted by section 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 and by section 7 of this Act shall not apply to in respect of any pleading filed before the commencement of Section 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure of (Amendment) Act, 1999 and Section 7 of this Act;"
8.

The High Court evidently committed illegality in relying upon the said provision."

5. The learned appellate Court dismissed the application only on the ground that after the amendment of Rule 17 Order 6 CPC, the parties were required to prove that inspite of due diligence, the party could not raise the matter before the commencement of the trial and accordingly dismissed the application.
I have heard the learned counsel for the parties and have gone through the records of the case.

6. At the outset, it may be observed that even the learned counsel for the respondents has fairly conceded that the order passed by the Court below dismissing the application only on the ground of due diligence cannot be supported in .
law.

He has fairly submitted that the amendment brought about by the Code of Civil Procedure by Amendment Act 22 of 2002 with effect from 01.07.2002, more particularly, provisions of Rule 17 Order 6 CPC would only operate prospectively and not to the proceedings already instituted.

7. It is also not in dispute that this legal position has already been set at rest by the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State Bank of Hyderabad v. Town Municipal of Council (2007) 1 SCC 765 wherein it was categorically held that by reason of Section 16(2) (b) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2002, the amendments carried out therein would only apply in respect of the suits rt which were filed after 01.07.2002.

25. Therefore, the learned First Appellate Court erred in rejecting the application on the ground that the plaintiffs had not applied for amendment before the commencement of trial.

26. The Learned First Appellate Court also held that the application was belatedly filed and the plaintiffs' case was that a specific portion of the land was purchased; therefore, it was not permissible for them to claim a share in the suit land.
These findings are supported by the record.

The plaintiffs had specifically asserted in para 1 of the plaint that they had purchased land measuring 2-5 bighas, out of Khasra No. 85(sic 83) measuring 5 bighas 8 Biswas through a registered sale deed.
The plaintiffs also filed an application for leading additional evidence before leaned First Appellate Court by placing a copy of the .

It was asserted in the application that the plaintiffs had purchased 2-5 bighas of land out of Khasra No. 83 denoted by Khasra No. 83/2 through a sale deed and tatima attached to it.
This area was depicted in mutation No. 218,which was subsequently of rejected.

Thus,
the plaintiffs came with a specific plea that they had purchased a specific portion of the land and they could not have prayed rt for the joint possession with the defendants.
Hence, the learned First Appellate Court had rightly held that the plaintiffs were taking inconsistent pleas and this was not permissible.

27. Hon'ble Supreme Court held in Ganesh Prasad v.
Rajeshwar Prasad, 2023 SCC OnLine SC 256 that inconsistent and contradictory pleas should not be allowed to be pleaded by the amendment.

It was observed:
37.
Thus, the Plaintiffs and Defendant are entitled to amend the plaint, written statement or file an additional written statement.
It is, however, subject to an exception that by the proposed amendment, an opposite party should not be subject to injustice and that any admission made in favour of the other party is not but wrong.

All amendments of the pleadings should be allowed liberally which are necessary for determination of the real controversies in the suit provided that the proposed amendment does not alter or substitute a new cause of action on the basis of which the original lis was raised or defence taken.
38. Inconsistent and contradictory allegations in negation to the admitted position of facts or mutually destructive .
allegations of facts should not be allowed to be incorporated by means of an amendment to the pleadings.
28. In the present case, the proposed amendment was contradictory to the stand taken by the plaintiffs.

The proposed amendment sought joint possession, whereas it was asserted in the plaint of that a specific portion of the land was purchased, therefore, the amendment was not necessary and would have caused a prejudice to the rt defendants which could not have been compensated in costs.
Besides this, it would displace the existing cause of action that a specific portion of the land was purchased and could not have been allowed.
Thus, there is no infirmity in disallowing the application for amendment.
Hence, the substantial question of law is answered accordingly.
Final Order
In view of the above, the present appeal fails and the same is dismissed.
Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

The plaintiffs did not raise any objection to the right of defendant no.1 as an owner in possession of the .
suit land.
Defendant no.2 was inducted as a tenant and mutation was rightly sanctioned in his favour.
Defendant No.1 is coming in open, peaceful, and continuous possession of the suit land to the knowledge of the plaintiffs and the public at large.
The plaintiffs had no locus standi to file the suit.
The ownership rights were conferred upon late Krishan Lal under the Himachal Pradesh Tenancy and Land Reforms Act.
The learned trial Court held that defendant no.1 had not disputed the sale deed in favour of the plaintiffs.
However,
the plaintiffs did not place any tatima on record to show the land purchased by them; therefore, no relief could be granted to them.
The defendants failed to prove their plea of adverse possession.
.
There was a distinction between a long possession and adverse possession.
Long possession cannot be equated to adverse possession.
The sale deed was not binding upon the rights of the plaintiffs to the extent of 2 bighas, 5 biswas.
The tenancy in favour of defendant no.2 by of defendant no.1 did not affect the rights of the plaintiffs.
The sale was of a specific portion of the land.
The plea taken by defendant no.1 regarding the sale deed being a sham transaction and that he remained in possession was not proved.
Hence, 1 bigha 1 biswas of land was acquired by the State of H.P. from the share of the plaintiffs and plaintiffs remained in possession of 1-4 bighas after the acquisition.
The suit of the plaintiffs was partly decreed and plaintiffs were held to be the owner in possession of land measuring 1-4 bighas bearing Khasra No. 83/2/2.
The sale of land measuring 1-4 bighas by Sher Singh in favour of defendant no.3 was held to be illegal.
Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Trial Court,
the present appeal has been filed asserting that the learned First Appellate Court erred in holding that 1-1 bighas of land was acquired from the share of the plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs filed an application under Order 6 Rule 17 of CPC for seeking the amendment of the plaint.

11. The appeal was admitted on the following substantial questions of law:-
"1.
Whether wrong assumptions have been drawn from the facts proved on record and the findings are based on inadmissible oral and documentary evidence particularly the letters stated to have been written by the appellant to Sher Singh,
which have been used without being proved.
2. Whether the District Judge was right in disallowing the amendment of the plaint and the findings are bad and against the well-settled principles for grant of an amendment which was necessary for determining the controversy between the parties?"
opennyai_summary.arguments:
It was laid down by the Delhi High Court in Rudnap Export-Import v.
rt Eastern Associates Co., 1983 SCC OnLine Del 136 = AIR 1984 Delhi 20 that no evidence is required to prove the document produced by the party and it can be read against him.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
19. No precedent to the contrary was brought to the notice of this Court; therefore, the learned First Appellate Court had rightly relied upon the document, which was produced by the plaintiffs and was put to of defendant no.1 in the cross-examination.
This application was opposed by the defendants by filing a written statement taking preliminary objection regarding lack of maintainability and the applicants being estopped by their act and conduct to file the present suit.
It was laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State Bank of Hyderabad v. Town Municipal Council, (2007) 1 SCC 765 =
2006 SCC OnLine SC 1322 that the proviso to Order 6 Rule 17 laying down that an amendment shall not be allowed after the commencement .
of Trial will not apply to the pleadings filed before 01.07.2022, the date of commencement of Code of Civil Procedure Amendment Act 2002.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Hence, the substantial question of law is answered accordingly.
Final Order
In view of the above, the present appeal fails and the same is dismissed.
Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
